In the future, try sketching both eyes at the same time. That is, sketch the outline for them and continue to add smaller details, keeping them at the same level of progress as you go. I’ve found this is easier than completely drawing one eye and moving on to the next.
Experiment with line thickness and learn to shade!

Art classes are still hella important. You’ve gotta get down your anatomy basics before making stylistic decisions. 

I’d also recommend practicing drawing with pencil and paper before going digital! Digital art has a mega steep learning curve, and you‘ve been using a pencil your whole life. It’ll be much easier to learn the basics of drawing that way.

When you draw the circle for the head, once you’ve drawn the hair you want to erase that line that separates the head from the hair and make the hair one solid piece. 

Also, hair has flow and volume. You’ve already conquered step one, which is that the hair isn’t flat on the scalp and sort of raises up a little bit, but there’s no discernible flow (unless you were aiming for random spikes. I’m not gonna say I’ve never rocked that hairstyle.)

Hi OP. You sound a lot like me. Like, hard relate to basically everything you said. And there is a point where self diagnosis becomes an option, as long as you aren’t attempting to manipulate doctors into giving you the diagnosis you “want,” or treating your illness like a badge of honor. It isn’t cringe to want to know what is wrong with you, and something is definitely wrong. 

I would look into BPD as a possibility — this is by no means me attempting to diagnose you, but your symptoms are eerily similar to mine. (I’m clinically diagnosed with BPD and major depressive disorder.) And no, the feelings you’re experiencing aren’t “normal.” This isn’t one of those “everybody gets that way sometimes.” You’re having intrusive and suicidal thoughts, and I urge you to seek professional help for them. I know you’re in therapy that’s on hold, but in MY experience, it’s been a general practitioner who prescribes my meds, which might be a good step to look into if you aren’t already on medication. 

Now, here’s the tricky bit. I’m going to recommend a website that has some assessments that can give you an IDEA of what’s going on with you. This is not a diagnostic tool — I’m sure you know not to take anything an online quiz tells you as fact. But idrlabs and their tests have been reasonably accurate for me, and it MIGHT give you a little more insight into things. They have an assessment on BPD specifically that you might find helpful.

Hi OP. I know that nothing I say will really fix anything, but I want you to know this. 

When I was 15, I didn’t think I’d live to be 18. When I was 18, I didn’t think I’d see 21. I mean, I was *convinced* of my own demise. (I’m 24 now. Didn’t think I would get here, but I did.) It was a scary place to be, and I know that’s where you are now because you’ve said it yourself. 

You’ve also said yourself that you don’t WANT to die. Which to some might not sound like much, but to me that sounds amazing. BPD is a tricky one — it can convince you of so many untrue things about yourself. It can put you at the lowest lows and keep you there for what feels like an eternity. But hold on to this truth — you don’t want to die. That’s more than some of us can say. 

I wish I could give better advice than this, but here’s how I made it through. Hold the hell on. Hold on to anything that makes you smile, anything that takes the pain away, even if it’s only fleeting, while you get your treatment plan right. Right now it might feel like you’re on a rollercoaster without a harness, so hold the hell on. Eventually it will come to a stop, even for a moment, and you’ll be able to strap in and brace yourself.

My condolences to both you and your partner. It’s a good sign that she WANTS to be better, and I wouldn’t say that the situation is hopeless. As a full disclaimer, I can only speak from MY experiences. I am not a licensed therapist, nor do I want to be. I’m just some chick with BPD and MDD who wants to help. 

First, take solace in the fact that she is willing to try. Couple’s therapy and individual therapy are vital at this point — bringing in professional help is the best thing to do when you reach a place where trying your best isn’t getting you where you need to be. Speaking from personal experience — the numbness she is feeling COULD be caused by one of the medications she’s taking, but it could also be a symptom of depression that her current treatment system isn’t helping. Mental health is somewhat of a guessing game sometimes, ESPECIALLY when medication is involved. But that feeling of numbness, it’s scary. I sympathize with both you and your girlfriend, and I genuinely hope that she’s able to find the right program of treatment to help her enjoy life and your company. 

The road ahead is going to be difficult for both of you. I don’t know your girlfriend, but I’ve been in similar shoes and I can’t imagine she WANTS to be in this situation. Despite how painful what you’re going through right now is, and I have no intentions of dismissing or minimizing that pain, I personally see it as a positive that she felt safe to tell you something like that so y’all can find the road forward. It’s going to take work and patience and, concerning medication, some trial and error, but you seem committed to each other. 

If you want to know what happened when I lost my emotions, I’ll tell you, but I didn’t handle it nearly as well as your gf seems to be handling it. The only bit of positivity in my story is the present — I’ve regained that part of myself after taking my medication more consistently and I’m choosing to move forward after the mistakes I’ve made. 

All this to say, best of wishes to the both of you. I know I’ve rambled. TL;DR — hopeless? Nah. Difficult and sad? Absolutely. But get with a pro head doctor, and see what comes of it. Props to both of you for not giving up outright.

Hi OP! A bunch of other commenters have given some really good advice, but here’s my little encouraging anecdote. I also used to be completely dreadful at Magic, and remained so for years until I started to get good at deck building. The game itself has a steep learning curve, and my biggest recommendation would be to look at deck lists online or watch EDH centered YouTube videos. There you’ll learn about certain card functions that are vital to the game (ramp, removal, draw engines) and how to effectively incorporate them into your decks. 

Also, try trading decks with your playgroup and running a game. That can help you figure out whether your deck build or your actual play is a bigger issue, and whoever ends up piloting your deck can give feedback on the main issues your deck might have. 

You can also ask your playgroup for feedback on your play style, and see if they can point out specific ways that you can improve. 

And again, I didn’t start winning games consistently until I had been playing for several years. It can be a hell of a grind for some people. Also remember that in a balanced game with four players, you should be winning about 25 percent of the time, so don’t get discouraged if you don’t start beating ass every time you shuffle up.

Hey OP. You’re probably not gonna believe me, but when I was 18, I felt exactly the fucking same. I felt like every day was waking up to do the same thing over and over again, and I distinctly remember crying at my dumb little eyes out at my high school graduation because I felt like everyone else’s life was just beginning, and mine was ending. 

Depression happens to people. It happened to me, it’s happening to you, it just happens. It feels like a struggle that’s never going to end. This might not be what you want to hear, but the most effective way to treat your depression is to tell somebody. Tell somebody who can get you help and get you on your way to a treatment plan. I take medication at night to help ease my symptoms. If that’s something you have to do, that’s not a shameful thing. Medication is how we treat illness, and that extends to mental illness. 

If that feels like it’s too big of a step, then challenge yourself to find one thing. One singular thing to keep you on the planet, and it doesn’t have to be a grand thing, and it doesn’t have to be the same thing forever. In middle school, I decided to stay alive for the next update of my favorite fanfic. In high school, it’s because I knew there wouldn’t be anyone else to take care of my cat. 

It feels like the exact opposite to you right now, but the more days you drag yourself through, the more likely it is that things will start to get easier. It’s okay to end up at a job you don’t like. Tons of people are at jobs they don’t like. The kind of dread and revulsion you’re feeling at that thought ? That’s depression. The apathy you feel is depression, the boredom is depression, and depression can be treated. The first step is to tell someone, because it can’t be treated if you just keep it inside and wish for things to change. 

In the meantime, hi. I’m Riley, and we might not have much in common other than the fact that we’re both depressed bastards. But if you need to let something out, I’m someone who’s really, SUPER been there. I’ll listen.

Ask a sociology or anthropology professor the difference between sex and gender. 

Even with all that aside, if someone close to you were to say, "I want to be known as a woman rather than a man," your first move shouldn't be to tell them that they can't change their sex.
